content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides a theoretical analysis of how deep neural networks learn in a hierarchical fashion. That is to say, it attempts to study the questions of a) how later layers of a network can use the features computed by the early layers to build higher-level features or make predictions, and b) how the quality of features in the early layers of a network can be improved from the information in the later layers in the network. They compare this hierarchical form of learning to layer-wise training, where the layers in a network are instantiated and trained one at a time, rather than trained jointly. For specific models and problem settings, the paper proves that training layers jointly improves the representations in lower layers of the network and that the model they consider can learn a specific class of functions in polynomial time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

The paper addresses a fundamental question about neural networks and attempts to rigorously prove the value of joint training in improving the feature representations in early layers of a neural network. This is an interesting question, and the paper attempts to answer it in a rigorous and exacting way.


**Weaknesses**

While this paper is theoretically interesting, there were a number of major areas in which I feel it needs improvement. First, the paper is extremely dense and difficult to follow in places. It has little high-level organization or self contained sections. Much of the findings of the paper are present only in the appendices, including all empirical experiments and most of the main theorems - with the only results stated in the main paper being limited to summarized versions of these theorems applied to extremely specific and limited cases. I would suggest that adding some empirical studies to the main paper and reorganizing it into self-contained sections might make it easier to follow. It would also be helpful if the paper more clearly stated exactly and specifically what the main results were in plain language and where they applied, as I found myself unsure about whether the full versions of the theorems were restricted to the specific problem setting discussed in the main paper or whether the full results in the appendices were more general. 

On that note, if I understand correctly, the results shown apply only to feedforward neural networks with quadratic activations and skip connections, trained with a specific variant of SGD, and applied to a knowledge distillation problem, where a learner network must learn to approximate another teacher network. Quadratic activations and skip connections are certainly not standard practice for feedforward networks, and making further limiting assumptions about the optimizer used as well as restricting the setting to knowledge distillation makes the result begin to feel very narrow. It is possible that the analysis shown in the paper may hold even when certain of these assumptions are relaxed, but if so that was not clear to me from reading the main body of the paper.

Third, I am somewhat unclear on what exactly the claimed significance of their result is. I had assumed that the paper would show that training layers jointly could provably approximate functions that layerwise training could not, or had provably better sample efficiency than layerwise training, but I do not believe I found any such proofs in the main body of the paper. All I found was allusions that the authors "do not know any other simple algorithm to learn [this problem class] in polynomial time". Can it be shown that no such algorithm exists for other training methods mentioned such as kernel approaches or layer-wise training?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

The paper was extremely dense and difficult to follow. It lacked high level organization (such as an introduction, conclusion, self-contained sections for separate sections of the result, etc...) and read mostly like one long and technical proof. It was difficult to discern exactly what the claimed results were, why they were significant, whether they were provably better than other methods and when exactly they held. Many of the main results were also stated only in the appendices, as well as all of the empirical experiments.

**Quality**

The theoretical analysis was rigorous, but I found it difficult to gauge exactly how significant the results actually were. Based on my understanding of the main paper, they seem limited enough in the scope of their application that I am not convinced they are a major contribution.

**Originality**

Yes, the work is novel.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the question asked by the paper is interesting and their analysis is technically sound and high-quality, but the clarity of the writing left something to be desired and I am unconvinced by the significance of the results shown. The paper needs major rewrites to make it easier to follow and more clearly demonstrate exactly what results it is claiming. The results also seem limited by a highly restrictive set of assumptions - specifically that the model in question is a feedforward neural network with quadratic activations and skip connections, that it uses a particular optimization method, and that it is applied to the setting of knowledge distillation.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: response to Reviewer Cr6L
content.comment:
We do acknowledge that our setting is limited to quadratic activation, a feedforward network trained with a variant of SGD. 

Yet, on the theory side, with all the limitations, our paper is still — to the best of our knowledge — the *first* paper that shows deep learning can learn some reasonable “deep class” – beyond low-degree polynomials. We have a theorem showing that no kernel method or one-hidden-layer NN with poly-activations can learn this class efficiently. Since proving lower bounds is generally hard, we are unsure how to prove lower bounds for layerwise training but have given intuitions for why we believe it does not work, and experiments to support that. 

Yet, on the practical side, with all the limitations, our paper is still — to the best of our knowledge — the *first* one that can be compatible with practical deep learning performance for instance for ResNet on the CIFAR data. We have shown that quadratic activation gives comparable performance to ReLU networks on the CIFAR data, and *much* better than kernel methods, two-layer ReLUs, or even layerwise training over ReLU networks — those will significantly lose accuracy on the CIFAR data.

Overall, we point out that our paper is not only a separation. As our title suggests, we focus on understanding the *inner workings* of neural networks as “how can deep learning perform hierarchical feature learning.” There are very few theory results that can help understanding the “inner working” of neural networks in terms of hierarchical feature learning (which is how deep learning is supposed to work). To truly understand this, we believe it is necessary to study **a setting where layerwise training fails** (or at least is not known to be possible) and backward feature correction plays a role. In this sense, we believe that our result is indeed significant, as we are **unaware of any prior (or even followup!) theory work** that can study backward feature correction in a deep setting.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tries to understand why and how deep learning performs hierarchical learning. More concretely, it aims to learn a large and expressive concept class in polynomial time and samples with a variant of SGD and layer-wise training. One of the key highlights of their method is to identify and exploit the backward feature correction property, which states that even if lower level layers tend to overfit, if they are trained together with a variant of SGD together with the higher level layers, they can actually correct the mistakes. As a lower bound, they also show that other well known methods like kernel methods, 2 layer networks cannot provably learn this class.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
It is one of the only papers that provably train a deep network in polynomial time/sample complexity and fit a reasonably expressive function class with super-constant depth, albeit with quadratic activations and a variant of SGD, which is not a standard algorithm that is commonly used. 

Clarifications:

1) I want to bring to your attention to cite the following papers, which are extremely relevant (Abbe et al. 2021, Abbe et al. 2022), shown below in the current ICLR paper.

References:
Abbe, Emmanuel, et al. "The staircase property: How hierarchical structure can guide deep learning." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34 (2021): 26989-27002.

Abbe, Emmanuel, Enric Boix Adsera, and Theodor Misiakiewicz. "The merged-staircase property: a necessary and nearly sufficient condition for sgd learning of sparse functions on two-layer neural networks." Conference on Learning Theory. PMLR, 2022.

Please compare and cite these papers in the current version. Especially Abbe et al. 2021, which learn a larger class of (upto degree $d$ polynomials, where $d$ is the input dimension) of Boolean functions, with a particular hierarchical structure, using a variant of Stochastic Block Coordinate Descent and layerwise training. 

2) Do the authors think one should use this variant of SGD while training, in practice or standard techniques (Adam etc)? Are the authors able to identify problems and datasets where their algorithm is better than the standard ones used in practice?

I am unable to access the zip file in the supplementary materials, as there might be some formatting issue.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5552 by Reviewer TrnG

content.title: response to Reviewer TrnG
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for pointing out these works. Please note those are follow-ups to our paper and they have even cited us. 

To compare with "the staircase property: how hierarchical structure can guide deep learning" by Abbe et al. which you concern the most, please note they did not study a “larger” class to this paper like you said. One can’t say they studied degree d and we studied degree log d so their class is bigger... Conversely, please note they studied a restrictive case, where layerwise training suffices to learn their class of functions (because they studied *Boolean* cube where lower-degree monomials are automatically "orthogonal" to higher-degree monomials, see literatures on Boolean analysis). As we emphasized **multiple times** in this paper, layerwise training performs poorly in practical deep learning. Our entire paper is to show how deep learning performs hierarchical learning **beyond** layerwise training, which requires backward feature correction. This is not captured by Abbe et al.

As for the complaint regarding the use of quadratic activations, we’d like to point out such activations are widely used for theoretical results (see the citations in our paper). We have even experimentally shown in the appendix that quadratic activation gives comparable performance to ReLU ones, and *much* better than layerwise training, kernel method, etc. In other words, yes we have studied a restricted, quadratic-activation setting but please note at the same time, we are also shooting for a higher bar — for instance as high as practical deep learning accuracies on the CIFAR data. In contrast, if you use kernel methods, two-layer ReLUs, or even layerwise training over ReLU networks, you will significantly lose accuracy on the CIFAR data.

(Sorry, it is unfortunate our supplementary material cannot be opened on some computers. We truly didn’t know this, but it is openable if you try softwares like 7zip or winrar.)

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The authors tackle a challenging problem in deep learning theory: how is it that
deep neural networks manage to learn hierarchical functions? They introduce a
new principle, called ``backward feature correction'', which they claim explains
how neural networks trained end-to-end on hierarchical tasks with SGD achieve a
performance better than non-hierarchical methods, such as greedy layer-wise
training or kernel methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I appreciate the effort the authors spent on giving an intuition for their
result with the example of a hierarchical polynomial. However, the authors
repeatedly stress that their main focus is not proving some separation between
deep neural networks and shallow methods from a representation point of view;
their focus appears to be on the dynamics. Hence the key question is how SGD
dynamics specifically achieve feature learning. Although I read the paper
carefully, I still do not understand exactly how the ``backward
feature-correction'' comes out of the SGD dynamics beyond some basic intution
that by training all the layers together with backprop, the layers will
co-evolve to fit the training data. So my main question for the authors would
be: how does backward feature correction emerge from SGD dynamics exactly?

The authors miss a few opportunities to clarify this. For example, in the
``Remark'' after the statement of their ``main message'' on p. 2, they refer to
experiments in Figs 3, 5, 10. But these figures just show receptive fields and
add arrows saying ``backward feature correction'', which did not help me
understand this concept further. While the experiments of the authors do show
that layer-wise training is inferior to end-to-end training (cf. for example
Figs 8 and 13), it did not become clear to me how backward feature-correction
accounts for this.

Similarly, in Fig. 6, you claim a back-and-forth in the learning of particular
layers of the network -- how did you arrive at this conclusion?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
## Some more specific questions

The presentation of the main result starting from Sec. 2 was confusing to me for
several reasons:

- Why the reparameterization? It first appears as if over-parameterization was
  important to learn the problem well (end of p. 4, beginning of p. 5 -- this
  would make sense from a practical point of view). Then however you
  re-parameterize in what appears to be a non-trivial way, keeping some
  weights fixed at their random initialisation, while you only compare what you
  call the "hidden features", which now seem to have again the same dimension as
  your teacher features. You say that the reparameterization is key for
  "efficient training", but I'm afraid the point is lost on me.
  
- Optimization: your results hold for a variant of SGD, as you state. While you
  state the algorithm in the appendix, I think the main text would benefit from
  a discussion of what changes you make to the standard SGD algorithm, and why
  they are important to prove your results.

## Smaller points

I appreciate the effort of the authors to write the article in an accessible
way, but I found the structure of the paper (main text containing only text,
with figures in appendix A, and details on the figures and subsequent
appendices) confusing as it lead to a lot of jumping around.  There is also a
number of typos in the manuscript, starting with the title ("How can deep
learning *perform* deep ...")
content.summary_of_the_review:
In summary, the authors should be lauded for tackling a key problem of deep
learning theory head-on. Unfortunately, after careful reading of the paper, I
still don't get a clear picture of their result, which is why I cannot recommend
the paper for acceptance as it stands. My evaluation along the other metrics
mostly reflect the fact that I didn't understand the chain of thought of the
authors, and are not definitive. I look forward to reading the clarifications of
the authors during the discussion period.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.title: response to Reviewer dQWY
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the very detailed review. You’ve given some good suggestions and we will listen to them in our future revisions. 

Meanwhile, for the intuition of how exactly SGD performs backward feature correction (i.e., improvement in lower layers after learning higher layers.), in this submitted submission, we have tried to explain it using an entire Section 1.2... Let us briefly summarize + rephrase it here.

Intuitively, if one has a function with both a low-degree part and high-degree part (which is a function over the low-degree part), then we want to learn the function in two steps. First learn the low-degree part and then learn a function on top of the low-degree part — to reduce the learning complexity compared to learning the high degree part from scratch.

However, how do we isolate the low-degree part from the original function? If we use a low-degree learner to fit the original function then it will over-fit. But, where does this over-fitting come from? It actually comes from the high-degree part – as we haven’t learned the high-degree part yet! Thus, if we train the high-degree part altogether, then as the high-degree part is learned more and more correctly, then the low-degree part can also be learned more and more correctly and eventually over-fitting can be eliminated. 

We also generalize this intuition to degree 2 + degree 4 + … + degree up to o(\log \log d). 


As for the re-parameterization, it is used to address the issue “richer representation by over-parameterization” (on page 4). The over-parameterized W is necessary by the discussions there. If one wants to understand more detailed (and technical) reasons for why we use K to distill W, it requires one to read our 4-paged sketched proof in appendix.  But we truly believe that this is only a technical difficulty and K is not needed in practice.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper tried to explain why deep neural networks could be applied for hierarchical learning tasks without introducing additional inductive biases.
This paper proposed the 'backward feature correction' principle, which claims that the errors in low levels could be automatically corrected when training low and high levels together.
With the help of backward feature correction principle, the over-fitting in lower-level layers could be reduced by using simple variants of SGD in polynomial time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The topic is fundamental and challenging. The proposed theory (though hard to follow) is solid and provides a new way of viewing deep neural networks.

Weakness:
No experiments are implemented to support the theory. At least some simulation results could be delivered. For example, the author use Eq. (1.1) to explain the effort of backward feature correction. Is it possible to observe the overfitting when training quadratic functions in two steps in the experiment? And is it possible to further train two layers together and observe the reduction of over-fitting? And in the case of 3 layers?

content.title: response to Reviewer vpM3
content.comment:
We thank the review for supporting that our work is fundamental and challenging. It is unfortunate that our supplementary material cannot be opened on some computers (we truly didn’t know this, but it is openable if you try softwares like 7zip or winrar). We have in fact included some extensive experiments in the appendix to support our findings and they happen to have answered your questions. 

Q: Is it possible to observe the overfitting when training quadratic functions in two steps in the experiment? 
A: Yes, we even visualized what such overfitting looks like in the appendix.

Q: And is it possible to further train two layers together and observe the reduction of over-fitting? And in the case of 3 layers?
A: Yes, in the appendix, not only we visualized how the over-fitting can be reduced, we even quantified for how much and how deep such backward correction is needed.

Moreover, among many other experiments, we empirically verified that layer-wise training without backward feature correction significantly underperforms training all the layers together, and the layer-wise training stops to improve accuracy after merely a few layers.
